chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (RA) narrated, saying: al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan ibn Aban narrated, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from 'Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: Hamzah ibn Humran narrated to me, saying: I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (AS) about ability, but he did not answer me. So I entered his presence at another time and said: May Allah make you upright, a matter has entered my heart regarding it which none can remove but something I hear from you. He said: Verily, what is in your heart will not harm you. I said: May Allah make you upright, for I say: Indeed, Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, has not burdened the servants except with what they can bear and what they are capable of, for they do not do anything of that except by the Will, Intent, Decree, and Power of Allah. He said: This is the religion of Allah in which I am and my forefathers are, or as he said. The Compiler of this book said: Allah's Intent and Will regarding obedience is the Command for it and the Pleasure in it, and regarding sins is the Prohibition from them and the Restriction from them through restraint and warning.
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia understanding of divine will and human ability in the context of not being burdened beyond capacity?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Tawhid* highlights the Shia doctrine of *istita'ah* (capability), affirming that human actions are performed through divine Will (*Mashi'ah*) and Intent (*Iradah*). The compiler, Shaykh al-Saduq, provides a crucial theological distinction: divine Will in obedience signifies command and pleasure, whereas in sins, it denotes prohibition and restraint, thereby reconciling human agency with divine decree. This clarification supports the Shia view that God does not create the sin itself but permits it through His will of allowance.
